Question 19 (Week 11): coding, the CLIP loss

Given normalized image embeddings img and text embeddings txt, both (N,d)(N,d)(N,d), and a learnable log temperature, write the symmetric CLIP loss. What is the loss of a random model?

Solution
python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def clip_loss(img, txt, logit_scale):
    # img, txt: (N, d), L2-normalized; logit_scale = exp(log(1/tau)), a scalar tensor
    logits = logit_scale * img @ txt.t()          # (N, N): entry (i, j) = similarity(image i, text j)
    labels = torch.arange(img.size(0), device=img.device)   # matching pairs are on the diagonal
    loss_i = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)       # image -> text
    loss_t = F.cross_entropy(logits.t(), labels)   # text -> image
    return (loss_i + loss_t) / 2

N, d = 8, 32
img = F.normalize(torch.randn(N, d), dim=-1)
txt = F.normalize(torch.randn(N, d), dim=-1)
print(clip_loss(img, txt, torch.tensor(1.0)).item())   # near log(8) = 2.08 for a random model

A random model gives about ln⁡N\ln NlnN (for N=32,768N=32{,}768N=32,768, about 10.4). Zero-shot classification then embeds the prompt "a photo of a {class}" for every class and picks the class with the highest cosine similarity to the image.

Question 20 (Week 11): inductive bias and data

Explain why a ViT trained from scratch on 10 000 images tends to lose to a ResNet, but wins when pretrained on hundreds of millions of images. How do DeiT and MAE change this picture?

Solution

Convolution hard-codes locality and translation equivariance; this prior is free information that makes learning efficient from small data. A ViT has only weak biases (patchification, and whatever is learned), so it must learn from data what a CNN assumes; with little data it overfits or underfits, with enough data the flexibility becomes an advantage and it scales better. DeiT recovers data efficiency on ImageNet-1k with heavy augmentation, regularization and distillation from a CNN teacher (the distillation token). MAE and other self-supervised methods supply a pretraining signal from unlabeled images, so the ViT can learn its own priors without labels. This is an empirical, not a proven, account.

Section E: Generative models (Weeks 12 and 13)

Question 21 (Week 12): the ELBO

Derive the ELBO using Jensen's inequality, and show that the gap equals DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∥pθ(z∣x))\KL(q_\phi(z|x)\|p_\theta(z|x))DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x)). For a diagonal Gaussian encoder N(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)N(μ,σ2) and prior N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1), give the closed form of the KL term and evaluate it for μ=1, σ=1\mu=1,\ \sigma=1μ=1, σ=1 in one dimension.

Solution

log⁡pθ(x)=log⁡∫pθ(x,z) dz=log⁡Eq[pθ(x,z)qϕ(z∣x)]≥Eq[log⁡pθ(x,z)qϕ(z∣x)]=Eq[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∥p(z))\log p_\theta(x)=\log\int p_\theta(x,z)\,dz=\log\E_{q}\Big[\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\Big]\ge\E_q\Big[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\Big]=\E_q[\log p_\theta(x|z)]-\KL(q_\phi(z|x)\|p(z))logpθ​(x)=log∫pθ​(x,z)dz=logEq​[qϕ​(z∣x)pθ​(x,z)​]≥Eq​[logqϕ​(z∣x)pθ​(x,z)​]=Eq​[logpθ​(x∣z)]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)) by Jensen (log is concave). Exactly, log⁡pθ(x)=ELBO+DKL(qϕ(z∣x)∥pθ(z∣x))\log p_\theta(x)=\mathrm{ELBO}+\KL(q_\phi(z|x)\|p_\theta(z|x))logpθ​(x)=ELBO+DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x)), so the gap is that KL and is zero when qqq equals the true posterior. For diagonal Gaussians DKL=12∑j(μj2+σj2−1−ln⁡σj2)\KL=\frac12\sum_j(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\ln\sigma_j^2)DKL​=21​∑j​(μj2​+σj2​−1−lnσj2​). For μ=1,σ=1\mu=1,\sigma=1μ=1,σ=1: 12(1+1−1−0)=0.5\frac12(1+1-1-0)=0.521​(1+1−1−0)=0.5.

Question 22 (Week 12): the reparameterization trick

Why can't we backpropagate through z∼N(μϕ,σϕ2)z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi,\sigma_\phi^2)z∼N(μϕ​,σϕ2​) directly, and how does z=μϕ+σϕϵz=\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\epsilonz=μϕ​+σϕ​ϵ fix it? Is it possible for discrete latents?

Solution

Sampling is a stochastic node, and the gradient of an expectation with respect to the distribution's parameters, ∇ϕEz∼qϕ[f(z)]\nabla_\phi\E_{z\sim q_\phi}[f(z)]∇ϕ​Ez∼qϕ​​[f(z)], is not an expectation of ∇f\nabla f∇f. Writing z=μϕ+σϕϵz=\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\epsilonz=μϕ​+σϕ​ϵ with ϵ∼N(0,1)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)ϵ∼N(0,1) moves the randomness to a parameter-free input, so ∇ϕEϵ[f(μϕ+σϕϵ)]=Eϵ[∇ϕf(⋅)]\nabla_\phi\E_\epsilon[f(\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\epsilon)]=\E_\epsilon[\nabla_\phi f(\cdot)]∇ϕ​Eϵ​[f(μϕ​+σϕ​ϵ)]=Eϵ​[∇ϕ​f(⋅)] and ordinary backprop works, with lower variance than score-function estimators. For discrete variables there is no differentiable reparameterization; one uses score-function (REINFORCE) estimators with baselines, or relaxations like Gumbel-softmax (biased), or straight-through estimators (as in VQ-VAE).

Question 23 (Week 12): the optimal discriminator

For fixed GGG with generated density pgp_gpg​, derive the optimal discriminator of the GAN objective and the value of the objective at the optimum in terms of the Jensen-Shannon divergence.

Solution

V(D,G)=∫[pdata(x)log⁡D(x)+pg(x)log⁡(1−D(x))]dxV(D,G)=\int\big[p_{data}(x)\log D(x)+p_g(x)\log(1-D(x))\big]dxV(D,G)=∫[pdata​(x)logD(x)+pg​(x)log(1−D(x))]dx. Pointwise, f(D)=alog⁡D+blog⁡(1−D)f(D)=a\log D+b\log(1-D)f(D)=alogD+blog(1−D) with a=pdata(x)a=p_{data}(x)a=pdata​(x), b=pg(x)b=p_g(x)b=pg​(x) is maximized where a/D−b/(1−D)=0a/D-b/(1-D)=0a/D−b/(1−D)=0, i.e. D∗(x)=pdata(x)pdata(x)+pg(x)D^*(x)=\dfrac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x)+p_g(x)}D∗(x)=pdata​(x)+pg​(x)pdata​(x)​. Substituting, V(D∗,G)=Epdatalog⁡pdatapdata+pg+Epglog⁡pgpdata+pg=−log⁡4+2 JSD(pdata∥pg)V(D^*,G)=\E_{p_{data}}\log\frac{p_{data}}{p_{data}+p_g}+\E_{p_g}\log\frac{p_g}{p_{data}+p_g}=-\log4+2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{data}\|p_g)V(D∗,G)=Epdata​​logpdata​+pg​pdata​​+Epg​​logpdata​+pg​pg​​=−log4+2JSD(pdata​∥pg​) (using DKL(p∥p+q2)\KL(p\|\tfrac{p+q}2)DKL​(p∥2p+q​) terms). So the generator minimizes the JSD, with global optimum pg=pdatap_g=p_{data}pg​=pdata​ giving D∗=1/2D^*=1/2D∗=1/2 and V=−log⁡4V=-\log4V=−log4. In practice the JSD gives vanishing gradients when the supports are disjoint, which motivates the Wasserstein distance.

Question 24 (Week 13): coding, the diffusion forward process

Derive q(xt∣x0)q(x_t|x_0)q(xt​∣x0​) in closed form for xt=1−βt xt−1+βt ϵtx_t=\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_txt​=1−βt​​xt−1​+βt​​ϵt​, then write q_sample and the training loss for a linear schedule.

Solution

Let αt=1−βt\alpha_t=1-\beta_tαt​=1−βt​ and αˉt=∏s≤tαs\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_sαˉt​=∏s≤t​αs​. Then xt=αtxt−1+1−αtϵtx_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\epsilon_txt​=αt​​xt−1​+1−αt​​ϵt​. Substituting xt−1x_{t-1}xt−1​ gives xt=αtαt−1xt−2+αt(1−αt−1)ϵt−1+1−αtϵtx_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}}x_{t-2}+\sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})}\epsilon_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\epsilon_txt​=αt​αt−1​​xt−2​+αt​(1−αt−1​)​ϵt−1​+1−αt​​ϵt​. The two noise terms are independent Gaussians with total variance αt(1−αt−1)+1−αt=1−αtαt−1\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})+1-\alpha_t=1-\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}αt​(1−αt−1​)+1−αt​=1−αt​αt−1​, so they merge into a single noise term. By induction xt=αˉtx0+1−αˉt ϵx_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilonxt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ, i.e. q(xt∣x0)=N(αˉtx0,(1−αˉt)I)q(x_t|x_0)=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I})q(xt​∣x0​)=N(αˉt​​x0​,(1−αˉt​)I).

python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

T = 1000
betas = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
alphas_bar = torch.cumprod(1.0 - betas, dim=0)           # (T,)

def q_sample(x0, t, noise):
    # x0: (B, C, H, W), t: (B,) long, noise: same shape as x0
    ab = alphas_bar[t].view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
    return ab.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - ab).sqrt() * noise

def diffusion_loss(model, x0):
    t = torch.randint(0, T, (x0.size(0),), device=x0.device)
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    x_t = q_sample(x0, t, noise)
    return F.mse_loss(model(x_t, t), noise)               # predict epsilon

x0 = torch.randn(4, 1, 8, 8)
t = torch.tensor([0, 10, 500, 999])
print(q_sample(x0, t, torch.randn_like(x0)).std(dim=(1, 2, 3)))

The printed standard deviations increase toward 1 as ttt grows: by t=Tt=Tt=T the signal is essentially destroyed.

Question 25 (Week 13): classifier-free guidance

State the guided noise prediction. What does increasing the guidance weight do to sample fidelity, diversity and sampling cost? Why does it work as a "sharpening" of the conditional distribution?

Solution

ϵ~=ϵθ(xt,∅)+(1+w)(ϵθ(xt,c)−ϵθ(xt,∅))\tilde\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)+(1+w)\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,c)-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)\big)ϵ~=ϵθ​(xt​,∅)+(1+w)(ϵθ​(xt​,c)−ϵθ​(xt​,∅)), equivalently (1+w)ϵθ(xt,c)−w ϵθ(xt,∅)(1+w)\epsilon_\theta(x_t,c)-w\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)(1+w)ϵθ​(xt​,c)−wϵθ​(xt​,∅). The model is trained with the condition randomly dropped (for example 10% of the time) so a single network provides both terms. Since ϵ\epsilonϵ is proportional to the negative score, the extrapolation corresponds to the score of p(x∣c) [p(c∣x)]wp(x|c)\,\big[p(c|x)\big]^{w}p(x∣c)[p(c∣x)]w up to normalization: it moves samples toward regions where the condition is more identifiable. Larger www increases fidelity and prompt adherence and reduces diversity (and can saturate colors and create artifacts); it doubles the network evaluations per step (conditional and unconditional passes, usually batched).

Question 26 (Weeks 12 and 13): choosing a generative family

A product team needs (i) image generation within 50 ms, (ii) exact bits-per-dimension for compression, (iii) a smooth latent for interpolation and editing. Which family would you pick for each, and what is the main drawback?

Solution

(i) A GAN (a single forward pass) or a distilled few-step diffusion model; the drawback is training instability and mode dropping for GANs, quality loss for aggressive distillation. (ii) An autoregressive model or normalizing flow gives exact log⁡p(x)\log p(x)logp(x); the drawback is slow sequential sampling (autoregressive) or architectural constraints (flows). (iii) A VAE (or the autoencoder of a latent diffusion model) has an encoder and a smooth latent space; the drawback is blurrier samples from the pixel-level likelihood, and posterior collapse risk. A diffusion model has no compact latent by itself and needs many steps to sample.

Section F: Graph neural networks (Week 14)

Question 27 (Week 14): permutation equivariance

Show that a GCN layer H′=σ(A^HW)\mathbf{H}'=\sigma(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W})H′=σ(A^HW) with A^=D~−1/2A~D~−1/2\hat{\mathbf{A}}=\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}A^=D~−1/2A~D~−1/2 is permutation equivariant, and explain why a graph-level readout must be invariant.

Solution

Relabel the nodes with a permutation matrix P\mathbf{P}P: A→PAP⊤\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\topA→PAP⊤, H→PH\mathbf{H}\to\mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}H→PH. Then A~→PA~P⊤\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{P}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{P}^\topA~→PA~P⊤ (since PIP⊤=I\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}\mathbf{P}^\top=\mathbf{I}PIP⊤=I), the degree matrix becomes PD~P⊤\mathbf{P}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{P}^\topPD~P⊤, and so A^→PA^P⊤\hat{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{P}\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{P}^\topA^→PA^P⊤. The layer outputs σ(PA^P⊤PHW)=P σ(A^HW)\sigma(\mathbf{P}\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W})=\mathbf{P}\,\sigma(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W})σ(PA^P⊤PHW)=Pσ(A^HW) because P⊤P=I\mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}P⊤P=I and σ\sigmaσ is elementwise: output rows are permuted the same way as the input. For a graph-level prediction the answer must not depend on the arbitrary node ordering, so the readout must be invariant (sum, mean, max or an attention-based pooling over nodes).

Question 28 (Week 14): aggregators and expressiveness

Give an example in which mean and max aggregation cannot distinguish two neighborhoods but sum can. What does this have to do with the Week 14 expressiveness result?

Solution

Neighborhood 1 has two neighbors with identical features aaa: multiset {a,a}\{a,a\}{a,a}; neighborhood 2 has one neighbor with feature aaa: {a}\{a\}{a}. Mean gives aaa in both cases, max gives aaa in both, but sum gives 2a2a2a versus aaa. The GIN analysis (Xu et al., 2019) shows that an injective multiset function is needed to match the discriminative power of the 1-WL isomorphism test, and sum (followed by an MLP) can be injective on countable multisets whereas mean and max cannot. Hence message-passing GNNs with mean or max are strictly weaker, and no standard message-passing GNN is more powerful than 1-WL.

Question 29 (Week 14): over-smoothing

Why do node representations become indistinguishable as you stack many GCN layers? Give two remedies and one tradeoff.

Solution

A GCN layer applies a low-pass filter A^\hat{\mathbf{A}}A^; repeated application A^kH\hat{\mathbf{A}}^k\mathbf{H}A^kH converges toward the dominant eigenvector of A^\hat{\mathbf{A}}A^ (constant on each connected component, scaled by degree), so node features lose discriminative information. Remedies: residual or skip connections (as in JKNet or GCNII), fewer layers, normalization layers such as PairNorm, DropEdge, and attention or jumping-knowledge readouts. The tradeoff: depth is what allows information to travel kkk hops, so cutting layers worsens long-range reasoning (over-squashing is the related, separate bottleneck); alternatives such as graph Transformers or rewiring address range directly.

Section G: Reinforcement learning (Week 15)

Question 30 (Week 15): TD targets by hand

A transition has r=1r=1r=1, γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, Q(s,a)=4Q(s,a)=4Q(s,a)=4. At s′s's′ the online network gives Q=[3,1]Q=[3,1]Q=[3,1] and the target network gives Q=[2,5]Q=[2,5]Q=[2,5] for the two actions. Compute the DQN target, the TD error and the Q-learning update with α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1 (tabular style), and the Double DQN target.

Solution

DQN target uses the target network's max: y=1+0.9⋅5=5.5y=1+0.9\cdot5=5.5y=1+0.9⋅5=5.5. TD error δ=5.5−4=1.5\delta=5.5-4=1.5δ=5.5−4=1.5, update Q←4+0.1⋅1.5=4.15Q\leftarrow4+0.1\cdot1.5=4.15Q←4+0.1⋅1.5=4.15. Double DQN chooses the action with the online network (arg⁡max⁡=\arg\max=argmax= action 0) and evaluates it with the target network: y=1+0.9⋅2=2.8y=1+0.9\cdot2=2.8y=1+0.9⋅2=2.8, so δ=−1.2\delta=-1.2δ=−1.2. Decoupling selection from evaluation removes the positive bias that the max over noisy estimates introduces.

Question 31 (Week 15): baselines in policy gradient

Show that subtracting a state-dependent baseline b(s)b(s)b(s) from the return does not bias the policy-gradient estimator, and say what the best baseline aims to do.

Solution

The extra term is Ea∼πθ[∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s) b(s)]=b(s)∑aπθ(a∣s)∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)=b(s)∑a∇θπθ(a∣s)=b(s)∇θ∑aπθ(a∣s)=b(s)∇θ1=0\E_{a\sim\pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a|s)\,b(s)]=b(s)\sum_a\pi_\theta(a|s)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a|s)=b(s)\sum_a\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(a|s)=b(s)\nabla_\theta\sum_a\pi_\theta(a|s)=b(s)\nabla_\theta1=0Ea∼πθ​​[∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)b(s)]=b(s)∑a​πθ​(a∣s)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)=b(s)∑a​∇θ​πθ​(a∣s)=b(s)∇θ​∑a​πθ​(a∣s)=b(s)∇θ​1=0. So the estimator stays unbiased (the baseline cannot depend on the action taken, or the argument fails). A good baseline reduces variance; the value function Vπ(s)V^\pi(s)Vπ(s) is the standard choice, and Gt−V(st)G_t-V(s_t)Gt​−V(st​) (or the advantage estimated by GAE) is the learning signal for actor-critic methods.

Question 32 (Week 15): the PPO clipped objective

With ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2ϵ=0.2 and probability ratio r=1.5r=1.5r=1.5, evaluate min⁡(rA^, clip(r,0.8,1.2)A^)\min(r\hat A,\ \mathrm{clip}(r,0.8,1.2)\hat A)min(rA^, clip(r,0.8,1.2)A^) for A^=+2\hat A=+2A^=+2 and for A^=−2\hat A=-2A^=−2, and say in which case the gradient is zero.

Solution

For A^=+2\hat A=+2A^=+2: rA^=3r\hat A=3rA^=3 and clip(r)A^=2.4\mathrm{clip}(r)\hat A=2.4clip(r)A^=2.4; the minimum is 2.42.42.4, the clipped term, which is constant in θ\thetaθ, so the gradient is zero: once the action's probability has already risen by more than 20%, there is no more incentive to increase it. For A^=−2\hat A=-2A^=−2: rA^=−3r\hat A=-3rA^=−3, clipped term =−2.4=-2.4=−2.4; the minimum is −3-3−3, the unclipped term, so the gradient flows and pushes the ratio back down. The objective is pessimistic: it removes the incentive for overly large policy changes in the profitable direction but not in the harmful one.

Question 33 (Week 15): find the bugs

The following DQN update has at least three problems. Find them.

python
q = qnet(s).gather(1, a)                    # s: (B, 4), a: (B, 1)
q_next = qnet(s2).max(dim=1).values          # (B,)
target = r + gamma * q_next                  # r: (B,)
loss = ((q - target) ** 2).mean()
loss.backward()
opt.step()
Solution

(1) The target is computed with the online network and with gradients, so the target moves with every update and gradients flow through it. Use a separate, slowly updated target network and torch.no_grad() (or .detach()). (2) Terminal transitions are not masked: the target must be r + gamma * (1 - done) * q_next. (3) Shape bug: q is (B,1)(B,1)(B,1) and target is (B,)(B,)(B,), so q - target broadcasts to (B,B)(B,B)(B,B) and silently averages the wrong quantity; use q.squeeze(1) or gather(...).squeeze(1). Also missing: opt.zero_grad() before backward(), and a Huber loss and gradient clipping would improve stability.

Section H: Efficiency and scale (Week 16)

Question 34 (Week 16): roofline reasoning

An accelerator has 300 TFLOP/s of fp16 compute and 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. (a) What is the ridge-point arithmetic intensity? (b) For an fp16 matrix product (M×K)⋅(K×N)(M\times K)\cdot(K\times N)(M×K)⋅(K×N) with M=N=K=4096M=N=K=4096M=N=K=4096, is it compute or memory bound? (c) What about the matrix-vector case M=1M=1M=1, K=N=4096K=N=4096K=N=4096, as in single-sequence decoding?

Solution

(a) Ridge point =3×1014/2×1012=150=3\times10^{14}/2\times10^{12}=150=3×1014/2×1012=150 FLOP/byte. (b) FLOPs =2MKN=2MKN=2MKN; bytes =2(MK+KN+MN)=2(MK+KN+MN)=2(MK+KN+MN) (2 bytes per fp16 element). For M=N=K=nM=N=K=nM=N=K=n: intensity =2n3/(6n2)=n/3=1365=2n^3/(6n^2)=n/3=1365=2n3/(6n2)=n/3=1365 FLOP/byte, well above 150, so compute bound. (c) For M=1M=1M=1: FLOPs =2KN≈3.4×107=2KN\approx3.4\times10^7=2KN≈3.4×107; bytes ≈2(K+KN+N)≈3.4×107\approx2(K+KN+N)\approx3.4\times10^7≈2(K+KN+N)≈3.4×107; intensity ≈1\approx1≈1 FLOP/byte, far below 150, so memory bound: the whole weight matrix is read to do one multiply-add per weight. Attainable throughput is about 1×21\times21×2 TFLOP/s, under 1% of peak, which is why decoding is bandwidth-limited and why batching, quantization and speculative decoding help.

Question 35 (Week 16): memory for training

How much memory do the parameters, gradients and Adam states take for a 7B-parameter model trained with mixed precision (bf16 compute, fp32 master weights and moments)? What does ZeRO stage 3 across 8 GPUs do to it, and what is not included?

Solution

Per parameter: 2 bytes (bf16 weight) +++ 2 bytes (bf16 gradient) +++ 4 (fp32 master weight) +++ 4 (mmm) +++ 4 (vvv) =16=16=16 bytes. For 7×1097\times10^97×109 parameters: 112×109112\times10^9112×109 bytes, about 112 GB (104 GiB). ZeRO-3 / FSDP shards all three (optimizer states, gradients, parameters) across the 8 GPUs: about 14 GB per GPU for these states. Not included: activations (which depend on batch, sequence length and checkpointing), temporary buffers and the communication needed to all-gather each layer's parameters just in time.

Question 36 (Week 16): gradient accumulation

(a) Write the accumulation loop to emulate a batch of 256 with micro-batches of 32. (b) For which layer does this differ from a true batch of 256?

Solution

(a)

python
accum = 8                                   # 256 / 32
opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
for i, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):         # loader yields micro-batches of 32
    loss = criterion(model(x), y) / accum   # divide so the summed gradient is the mean
    loss.backward()                         # gradients add up in .grad
    if (i + 1) % accum == 0:
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

(b) For layers whose forward pass couples the examples in the batch: BatchNorm computes statistics from each micro-batch of 32, not 256, and is therefore not equivalent (use GroupNorm or LayerNorm, or sync/accumulate statistics). Dropout masks and in-batch contrastive losses (CLIP, InfoNCE with in-batch negatives) also differ: the number of negatives is that of the micro-batch.

Section I: Trustworthy deep learning (Week 17)

Question 37 (Week 17): FGSM from first principles

Derive FGSM from a first-order Taylor expansion of the loss for an ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ budget ϵ\epsilonϵ, and state the corresponding step for an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ budget.

Solution

L(x+δ)≈L(x)+g⊤δ\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta})\approx\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{x})+\boldsymbol{g}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}L(x+δ)≈L(x)+g⊤δ with g=∇xL\boldsymbol{g}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L}g=∇x​L. Maximize over ∥δ∥∞≤ϵ\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_\infty\le\epsilon∥δ∥∞​≤ϵ: each coordinate is independent and giδig_i\delta_igi​δi​ is maximized by δi=ϵ sign(gi)\delta_i=\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(g_i)δi​=ϵsign(gi​), giving the increase ϵ∥g∥1\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_1ϵ∥g∥1​. For an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ ball the maximizer is δ=ϵ g/∥g∥2\boldsymbol{\delta}=\epsilon\,\boldsymbol{g}/\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2δ=ϵg/∥g∥2​ (Cauchy-Schwarz) with increase ϵ∥g∥2\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2ϵ∥g∥2​. The linearity explanation notes that in ddd dimensions the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of a gradient can be large even for a tiny per-coordinate budget, so many small coordinated changes add up.

Question 38 (Week 17): expected calibration error

A classifier makes 10 predictions in two confidence bins. Bin A has 4 predictions with mean confidence 0.9 and 3 correct. Bin B has 6 predictions with mean confidence 0.6 and 3 correct. Compute the ECE and say whether the model is over- or underconfident.

Solution

Bin A: accuracy 0.750.750.75, confidence 0.900.900.90, gap 0.150.150.15, weight 0.40.40.4. Bin B: accuracy 0.500.500.50, confidence 0.600.600.60, gap 0.100.100.10, weight 0.60.60.6. ECE=0.4⋅0.15+0.6⋅0.10=0.06+0.06=0.12\mathrm{ECE}=0.4\cdot0.15+0.6\cdot0.10=0.06+0.06=0.12ECE=0.4⋅0.15+0.6⋅0.10=0.06+0.06=0.12. In both bins confidence exceeds accuracy: overconfident. Temperature scaling with T>1T>1T>1 would soften the probabilities and reduce the gap without changing accuracy.

Question 39 (Week 17): split conformal prediction

You have n=19n=19n=19 calibration nonconformity scores and want 90% coverage. (a) Which order statistic is the threshold? (b) State the guarantee and its assumption. (c) Why is it only a marginal guarantee?

Solution

(a) k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉=⌈20⋅0.9⌉=18k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil=\lceil20\cdot0.9\rceil=18k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉=⌈20⋅0.9⌉=18: use the 18th smallest score as the threshold q^\hat qq^​ and include in the prediction set every label whose score is at most q^\hat qq^​. (b) If the calibration and test points are exchangeable, P(Yn+1∈C(Xn+1))≥1−αP(Y_{n+1}\in C(X_{n+1}))\ge1-\alphaP(Yn+1​∈C(Xn+1​))≥1−α; this holds for any model and any finite nnn (the proof: the test score is equally likely to be at any rank among the n+1n+1n+1 scores). (c) The probability is over the draw of calibration set and test point jointly, so coverage can still be much lower for particular inputs, classes or subgroups; conditional coverage is not guaranteed. Distribution shift also breaks exchangeability.

Question 40 (Week 17): DP-SGD

Describe one DP-SGD step. Why must per-example gradients be clipped, and what is the role of the noise multiplier? What does the privacy budget depend on?

Solution

For a sampled batch: compute each example's gradient gig_igi​, clip it to norm at most CCC (gˉi=gi/max⁡(1,∥gi∥/C)\bar g_i=g_i/\max(1,\norm{g_i}/C)gˉ​i​=gi​/max(1,∥gi​∥/C)), sum, add Gaussian noise N(0,σ2C2I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2C^2\mathbf{I})N(0,σ2C2I), divide by the batch size, and take an optimizer step. Clipping bounds the influence (sensitivity) of any single example on the sum by CCC; without a bound no finite noise level could hide an individual. The noise scale is proportional to σC\sigma CσC; larger σ\sigmaσ means more privacy and lower accuracy. The (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)(ε,δ) guarantee follows from composition over steps with amplification by subsampling, computed by a moments or Renyi accountant, and depends on σ\sigmaσ, the sampling rate q=B/Nq=B/Nq=B/N, the number of steps, and δ\deltaδ. Training longer or with a smaller σ\sigmaσ spends more budget.

Question 41 (Week 17): fairness criteria

Define demographic parity and equalized odds. Explain why, when base rates differ between groups, a non-perfect classifier cannot satisfy calibration within groups and equal false positive and false negative rates at once.

Solution

Demographic parity: P(Y^=1∣A=a)P(\hat Y=1|A=a)P(Y^=1∣A=a) is equal across groups aaa. Equalized odds: P(Y^=1∣Y=y,A=a)P(\hat Y=1|Y=y,A=a)P(Y^=1∣Y=y,A=a) is equal across groups for y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1} (equal TPR and FPR). Calibration within groups (predictive parity): P(Y=1∣S=s,A=a)P(Y=1|S=s,A=a)P(Y=1∣S=s,A=a) is the same function of the score for every group. Chouldechova (2017) and Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) show that with unequal base rates pa≠pbp_a\ne p_bpa​=pb​ and imperfect prediction these conditions are mutually incompatible: for example, the identity FPR=p1−p1−PPVPPVTPR\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{p}{1-p}\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\mathrm{TPR}FPR=1−pp​PPV1−PPV​TPR ties the error rates to the base rate ppp, so equal PPV and equal TPR force unequal FPR. The choice of criterion is therefore a policy decision, not a purely technical one.

Question 42 (Week 17): coding, temperature scaling

Fit a temperature on validation logits by minimizing NLL, and explain why the test accuracy cannot change.

Solution
python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def fit_temperature(logits, labels):
    # logits: (N, K) from a frozen model on a held-out validation set
    log_T = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)          # parametrize T = exp(log_T) > 0
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([log_T], lr=0.1, max_iter=100)
    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits / log_T.exp(), labels)
        loss.backward()
        return loss
    opt.step(closure)
    return log_T.exp().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
logits = torch.randn(1000, 5) * 3                        # overconfident toy logits
labels = torch.randint(0, 5, (1000,))
print(fit_temperature(logits, labels))                   # T > 1: random labels, so it softens a lot

Dividing all logits by T>0T>0T>0 preserves their order, hence the argmax and the accuracy. Only the confidence changes. Fit on validation data, never on the test set.

Section J: Reporting and the scientific method (Week 18)

Question 43 (Week 18): is the claim supported?

A team reports test accuracy of method A as 71.2, 70.8, 71.5 and of method B as 71.9, 71.0, 72.1 (three seeds each) and concludes "B is better". Evaluate the claim.

Solution

Means: xˉA=71.17\bar x_A=71.17xˉA​=71.17, xˉB=71.67\bar x_B=71.67xˉB​=71.67, a gap of 0.500.500.50. Sample standard deviations: sA≈0.35s_A\approx0.35sA​≈0.35, sB≈0.59s_B\approx0.59sB​≈0.59. The standard error of the difference is 0.352/3+0.592/3≈0.39\sqrt{0.35^2/3+0.59^2/3}\approx0.390.352/3+0.592/3​≈0.39, so Welch's t≈0.50/0.39≈1.3t\approx0.50/0.39\approx1.3t≈0.50/0.39≈1.3 with about 3.3 degrees of freedom; the 5% critical value is around 3. The difference is not significant, and each method's own 95% interval (±4.30 s/3\pm4.30\,s/\sqrt3±4.30s/3​, about ±0.87\pm0.87±0.87 for A and ±1.46\pm1.46±1.46 for B) comfortably contains the other's mean. The right statement is "B is higher in these three runs, but three seeds cannot distinguish a 0.5-point gap from noise." The fix is more seeds (the explorer above shows how quickly the interval narrows), a paired analysis if the seeds are matched, and a check that both methods got the same tuning effort.

Exercises

The practice exam above is the main exercise set for this week. These additional exercises focus on the project and on the cross-cutting skills.

Exercise 1: audit your own project (conceptual)

Fill in the sentence "We show that ___, by measuring ___, against ___." for your project. Then list the three weakest points of your evidence and what experiment would address each.

Solution

There is no single answer; a good response is specific. Example: "We show that cosine decay with warmup improves a small ViT on CIFAR-10 by about 1 point (claim), by measuring top-1 test accuracy over 5 seeds with a 95% interval (metric), against the same ViT with a constant learning rate and a ResNet-18 baseline (baselines)." Typical weak points and fixes: only 3 seeds (run 5 to 10); the baseline learning rate was not tuned (give it the same search budget); the hyperparameters were chosen by looking at test accuracy (re-select on a validation split and evaluate once on test); no failure analysis (inspect and slice the 50 worst examples).

Exercise 2: sample size for a target interval (derivation)

Your per-seed standard deviation is about σ=0.6\sigma=0.6σ=0.6 points. Using the normal approximation (multiplier 1.96), how many seeds do you need for a 95% confidence interval of half-width at most 0.30.30.3 points? Is that the number you need to detect a true gap of 0.3 points between two methods?

Solution

Half-width =1.96 σ/n≤0.3⇒n≥1.96⋅0.6/0.3=3.92⇒n≥15.4=1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\le0.3\Rightarrow\sqrt n\ge1.96\cdot0.6/0.3=3.92\Rightarrow n\ge15.4=1.96σ/n​≤0.3⇒n​≥1.96⋅0.6/0.3=3.92⇒n≥15.4, so n=16n=16n=16 (using the ttt multiplier for such nnn gives about 17). For detecting a difference between two independent methods, the standard error of the gap is σ2/n\sigma\sqrt{2/n}σ2/n​, so to have the interval half-width of the gap below the gap itself (0.30.30.3) you need 1.96⋅0.62/n≤0.31.96\cdot0.6\sqrt{2/n}\le0.31.96⋅0.62/n​≤0.3, i.e. n≥2⋅15.4≈31n\ge2\cdot15.4\approx31n≥2⋅15.4≈31 seeds per method. A reliable detection (power 80%) needs roughly a factor of 2 more than that threshold-type requirement. This is why small effects are expensive to establish and why paired designs or larger effects are preferred.

Exercise 3: coding, an ablation grid with seeds

Extend the Run harness so that a function sweep(train_fn, configs, seeds) runs every configuration for every seed and prints a table of mean, standard deviation and CI per configuration. Which seeds should you share across configurations?

Solution
python
import itertools
from dataclasses import replace
import numpy as np
from tracking import Config, Run
from seed_stats import summarize

def sweep(train_fn, configs, seeds):
    """train_fn(cfg, run) -> final test metric. Returns {config name: [metric per seed]}."""
    results = {}
    for cfg, seed in itertools.product(configs, seeds):
        c = replace(cfg, seed=seed)
        run = Run(c)
        metric = train_fn(c, run)
        run.finish(test_metric=metric)
        results.setdefault(cfg.name, []).append(metric)
    print(f"{'config':<20}{'mean':>8}{'std':>8}{'ci95':>8}")
    for name, xs in results.items():
        s = summarize(xs)
        print(f"{name:<20}{s['mean']:>8.2f}{s['std']:>8.2f}{s['ci_half']:>8.2f}")
    return results

# Example with a fake training function whose metric depends on lr and the seed
def fake_train(cfg, run):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(cfg.seed)
    return 90 + (0.5 if cfg.lr == 3e-4 else 0.0) + 0.4 * rng.normal()

cfgs = [Config(name="lr1e-3", lr=1e-3), Config(name="lr3e-4", lr=3e-4)]
sweep(fake_train, cfgs, seeds=range(5))

Use the same list of seeds for every configuration, so comparisons can be paired and differences in data order or initialization do not masquerade as differences between configurations.

Exercise 4: reproduce a figure (challenging)

Choose one published figure or table from a Week 9 to 17 paper that your hardware can reproduce at small scale (for example, the effect of 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ scaling on attention entropy, the Wasserstein-versus-JS gradient behavior on disjoint supports, or temperature-scaling reliability diagrams). Plan the reproduction: what is the claim, what can you scale down without changing its meaning, what would count as success, and what would you report if you failed?

Solution

A good plan states the claim in one sentence and the invariants you must keep (for the attention example: unit-variance queries and keys, a range of dkd_kdk​, softmax over the same number of positions) and the things you can shrink (the sequence length, the number of heads, the training length). Success criterion: a quantitative one, such as "the mean attention entropy stays near log⁡T\log TlogT with the scaling and falls toward 0 without it as dkd_kdk​ grows from 16 to 1024, over 10 random draws". If the figure does not reproduce, report it as a finding with the details: which settings differ from the paper, which you could not determine from the text, and what you tried. A failed reproduction with a careful log is a legitimate and useful result; an unexamined mismatch is not.

Exercise 5: design the evaluation (what would happen if...)

You fine-tune a pretrained model on a 5,000-example dataset and report test accuracy from the best validation checkpoint chosen over 30 hyperparameter configurations, each with one seed. A reviewer suspects the reported gain over the baseline is inflated. List three mechanisms that could inflate it and one protocol that removes them.

Solution

(1) Selection bias: the best of 30 noisy single-seed runs is on average higher than the true performance of the recipe (winner's curse), so the reported number is optimistic even on a validation set, and more so if selection is done on test data. (2) The baseline received less tuning, so part of the gap is tuning effort. (3) Test set noise: with a small test set the standard error of accuracy is large, and any small difference can be noise; leakage between pretraining data and the test set is also possible. Protocol: split a separate validation set; choose hyperparameters on it with a fixed budget for every method; retrain the chosen configuration with 5 or more seeds; evaluate once on the test set; report mean and interval for both methods; optionally use nested cross-validation if data are scarce.

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Mistakes that cost points on the final project and in the exam:

  • Single-seed claims. Symptom: "B beats A by 0.3". Fix: at least 3 to 5 seeds, intervals, and cautious wording.
  • Baseline neglect. Symptom: huge gains over a default-hyperparameter baseline. Fix: tune the baseline with the same budget; include a simple non-deep baseline.
  • Test-set contamination. Symptoms: validation and test curves that are suspiciously close, or results that vanish on fresh data. Fix: freeze the test set, look at it once, check for duplicates across splits.
  • Cherry-picked figures. Qualitative examples that are best-case. Fix: random, uncurated examples and failure cases.
  • An over-long talk. Symptom: the last three slides are rushed. Fix: rehearse with a timer and cut content.
  • Unexplained numbers. A table with no stated metric, split or seed count. Fix: captions that say what, on which data, over how many runs.
  • A README that does not run. Symptom: missing data download step, unpinned versions. Fix: a clean-clone test on another machine or a fresh Colab session.
  • Exam: skipping units and shapes. Write the shape of every tensor and the units of every quantity; most calculation errors show up there.
  • Exam: derivations without definitions. State what every symbol means; partial credit depends on it.
  • Exam: memorizing without understanding. Many questions change one assumption (for example, "what if the layer used a sigmoid instead of ReLU?"); practice asking that question of every result.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • A project talk makes one claim, spends most of its time on evidence, and shows uncertainty and failures. Twelve minutes means eight to ten slides.
  • A fair comparison needs a strong baseline with equal tuning effort, ablations that isolate each component, and several seeds. Intervals shrink only like 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​; a single seed can pick the wrong winner a third of the time for a 0.3-point effect.
  • Report mean and interval over seeds with the multiplier tn−1,0.975t_{n-1,0.975}tn−1,0.975​, say what the error bar is, and consider paired analyses and test-set sampling error separately.
  • Reproducibility means recording code, config, data, environment and randomness together for every run, and shipping a README that regenerates every number in the report.
  • The course in one line: a loss (usually a log-likelihood or bound), a parameterized function with the right inductive bias, an optimizer, data, and the scientific discipline to know whether it worked.
  • Debug from simple to complex: overfit one batch, check the initial loss, inspect data, then tune.
  • To study for the exam, retrieve rather than reread: derive, compute and code from a blank page, and fix what you miss.

Part IV: next steps

How to read research papers

By now you have read and presented papers (see How to read and present a paper). The skill that separates efficient readers from exhausted ones is multi-pass reading, which follows Keshav's "How to Read a Paper" (2007).

During pass 2 keep a short written summary in a fixed template; it forces understanding and makes the paper searchable later:

  1. Problem. What is being solved, and why is it hard?
  2. Key idea. One or two sentences, in your own words.
  3. Method. The model, loss and training procedure, with notation.
  4. Evidence. Which experiments support which claims? What are the baselines, the number of seeds, and the effect size relative to noise?
  5. Limitations. Stated by the authors and found by you.
  6. Connections. Which course weeks and other papers does it relate to?

Questions to ask in the critique pass: Is the baseline strong and tuned? Is the compute budget matched? Does the ablation isolate the claimed cause? Is the improvement larger than seed noise? Does the benchmark measure what the title claims? Could the test set have been seen in pretraining? Are there negative results hidden in the appendix? What would falsify the central claim?

Practical advice: read the abstract, the figures and the conclusion first; read the appendix for hyperparameters and extra results; follow the references of a paper you like backwards (what it builds on) and the citations forwards (what built on it, via Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar). Keep a reading log. Join or start a reading group: explaining a paper aloud exposes gaps better than rereading. Skim arXiv regularly (the daily lists in cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CV), but prefer depth over breadth; a handful of papers read well beats fifty skimmed.

Reproducing a paper

Reproducing a result is the best exercise after this course. It forces you to confront every detail that papers omit. A workable process:

  1. Choose well. Pick a paper with a small-scale core result (a figure you can regenerate in hours on one GPU), public code or at least a clear description, and a clear success criterion. Avoid papers whose headline result needs thousands of GPU-hours.
  2. Define success first. Write down which numbers or curves you expect and the tolerance (relative to seed variance) before you run anything.
  3. Start from the simplest working version and verify each component against a known value: shapes, parameter counts (the paper often states them), the initial loss, and a one-batch overfit.
  4. Match the details that matter: data splits and preprocessing, initialization, optimizer settings, schedule, batch size, evaluation protocol and metric implementation. Differences here explain most failed reproductions.
  5. Use reference code as a check, not a copy. Read the official implementation after your own attempt to find discrepancies, and cite it. Course policy requires disclosure of external code.
  6. Log everything with the harness from this page, run several seeds, and keep a "differences from the paper" list.
  7. Report honestly, including partial success. Discrepancies, such as a metric that moves by 0.5 points because of a data-loading detail, are valuable to the community.

A useful ladder of difficulty: reproduce a figure from a course reading (a day), reproduce a small benchmark number (a week), reproduce an ablation from a recent paper (a few weeks), and extend it with one new experiment (a project).

Contributing to open source

Open-source contributions are an excellent way to learn how real systems are built and to become visible to future collaborators and employers. Start small and be patient.

  • Pick a library you use, such as PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and Datasets, timm, PyTorch Geometric, Stable-Baselines3, scikit-learn, or this course site.
  • Begin with documentation: fix typos, clarify an unclear example, add a missing docstring, or translate a page. These are welcome and teach you the workflow.
  • Look for issues labeled "good first issue" or "help wanted," and comment before you start to avoid duplicated work.
  • Reproduce the bug first in a minimal script. A minimal, reproducible bug report is itself a contribution.
  • Follow the contribution guide: coding style, tests, commit message format, and the review process. Keep pull requests small and focused, include a test, and respond to review comments politely and quickly.
  • Add something you built: a model implementation with a verified result, a tutorial notebook, a benchmark script. Maintainers value correctness and clarity over novelty.
  • Release your project code properly: a license, a README that works, version pins, and a citation entry.

Career paths

Deep learning work has several overlapping roles. They emphasize different skills; you can move between them, and many people do.

Path Typical work Skills to emphasize How to prepare
Research (academic or industrial lab) Posing new questions, designing experiments, writing papers Strong math, rigorous experimentation, writing, depth in one area Reproduce and extend papers, a thesis or project with an advisor, workshops, then conference submissions
Applied ML or data science Turning a business problem into a model with measurable impact Problem framing, data understanding, baselines, evaluation, communication Projects on real, messy data; Kaggle-style competitions as practice; domain knowledge
ML engineering and MLOps Training and serving models at scale, pipelines, monitoring Software engineering, systems, GPUs, distributed training, testing Strong coding, profiling and deployment practice (Week 16), contributing to open-source infrastructure
Specialist roles Safety and evaluation, interpretability, data and annotation quality, product and policy Domain-specific rigor, statistics, ethics (Week 17) Projects that stress-test models; reading and writing evaluations and audits

General advice: build a small public portfolio of two or three well-documented projects (code, a short write-up, and results with honest error bars), and be able to explain every choice in them. Learn to communicate with non-specialists. Stay curious about the data: most real-world gains come from better data, evaluation and problem framing, rather than a new architecture. Be wary of hype in either direction, and keep checking claims, including your own, against evidence.

Further courses and resources

  • Courses: Stanford CS231n (convolutional networks for visual recognition), CS224n (NLP with deep learning), CS224W (machine learning with graphs), CS236 (deep generative models); Berkeley CS285 (deep reinforcement learning); MIT 6.S191 (introduction to deep learning); fast.ai Practical Deep Learning; Andrej Karpathy's "Neural Networks: Zero to Hero" video series; the Hugging Face courses and documentation.
  • Fundamentals worth strengthening: probability and statistics (Murphy; Bishop's Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning), optimization (Boyd and Vandenberghe's Convex Optimization), linear algebra (Strang), and information theory (Cover and Thomas).
  • Where papers appear: NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR for general machine learning; CVPR, ICCV and ECCV for vision; ACL and EMNLP for language; plus arXiv and OpenReview (which also hosts peer reviews, an excellent way to learn how papers are judged).
  • Practice: build things end to end; enter a competition with a time limit; write a blog post explaining one paper; teach this course's material to someone else.
  • Keep your toolchain current: the specific libraries will change over the years, but the habits in this course (small experiments, baselines, seeds, logs, honesty) will not.

Further reading

The reading list above is the reading list for the week. If you read only three things: Keshav (2007) on reading papers, Henderson et al. (2018) on reproducibility and the effect of seeds in deep RL, and Karpathy's recipe for training neural networks (2019).
